conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds continue—tacrolimus, prednisone, sevelamer, the rest. Just no warfarin until your PCP advises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you this afternoon. Your fever is gone, pain is resolved, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my PCP and nephrologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and call us if you develop redness, fever, or belly pain again. Keep the catheter site clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll take the laxatives regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve made great progress. We’ll send all instructions to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Your vitals are stable, and your exam looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. You’re cleared to go home. A nurse will review your meds and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. Remember: no warfarin, finish the antibiotics, and keep up the bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll get the INRs checked three times a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your PCP has all the details. Call if anything changes before your appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine was a bit dark. That’s likely from dehydration or old blood. Keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried if it stays brown?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it persists or you feel worse, call your nephrologist. But it’s likely benign given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The transport team will take you out shortly. Feel better!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’m glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with body aches and a low-grade temperature after dialysis today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been hurting all over—head, back, legs, arms. And my stomach pain came back too, worse than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned it started after hemodialysis. Any fever at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just 99.6. But I felt chills. And I threw up once this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check for infection and see if this is related to your recent catheter or transplant. Let’s get your vitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is high, likely from pain. We’ll give you a small dose of IV morphine to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I can’t take oral pain meds—they make me sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage that. Your INR is high at 6.7, so we gave you vitamin K by mouth to reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My INR has been all over the place. I restarted Coumadin last week—6mg, then 5, then 4.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might explain it. We’ll adjust your warfarin carefully. We’re also checking your transplant function and for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show mild anemia and low white count, but no infection signs. CRP is elevated, suggesting inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not clearly. Your peritoneal fluid showed only 31 white cells—no infection. Cultures are negative. But your chest X-ray shows a new infiltrate in the left lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have a cough or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes pneumonia can be silent, especially with your history. We’ll treat it with antibiotics—azithromycin, safer with your warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But my stomach pain—could it be from the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted transplant surgery. Your abdomen is soft, no signs of rejection. Pain might be from constipation—we saw fecal loading on the abdominal X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I had a normal bowel movement yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes constipation causes liquid stool around a blockage. We’ll increase your Miralax and senna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV test came back negative—good, no viral infection. Peritoneal fluid culture is also negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I keep getting these fevers and pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Could be from inflammation, constipation, or even a reaction to dialysis. We’re involving GI and pain specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had dialysis this morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still achy. Stomach pain comes and goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team suggests trying rectal morphine suppositories—they may cause less nausea than oral pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try anything. But I don’t want IV—too slow with the drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start the suppository and see how it works. We also want to do a CT scan to rule out mesenteric ischemia—poor blood flow to the gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those tests before. They said my arteries were too calcified to see well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This CT uses contrast and better imaging. It should clarify things. We’ll schedule it for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. Good news—no bowel ischemia. Your arteries are calcified but open. No blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The main finding is significant constipation—fecal load in the colon. That’s likely the cause. Also, you have a small liver cyst and a right adnexal cyst, but both look stable and benign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had the pelvic cyst for years. My gynecologist said it’s fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it hasn’t changed. But we recommend follow-up with your gynecologist to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fluid around my lung?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a right-sided pleural effusion. It’s not new, and you’re not short of breath, so we’ll monitor it. Repeat chest X-ray in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 7.5 yesterday—too high. We reduced warfarin to 1mg. Today it’s 3.2—much better. But then it dropped to 2.0, so we increased it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s so hard to keep it stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with antibiotics. Levofloxacin can raise INR. We switched to azithromycin to avoid that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotic change helped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. Your INR is now 3.7 on 4mg warfarin. We’ll send you home on 2mg daily and close INR monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed your antibiotic course. The pneumonia is resolving. Your pain is better with the suppositories and bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been nauseated with the rectal morphine. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re adding gabapentin for nerve pain support. And you’ll continue Miralax and senna. Use tap water enemas if you don’t have a full bowel movement daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. What about the pain if it comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the morphine suppository as needed. Avoid ER visits unless severe. Your local pharmacy will have the suppositories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready to go home. Your pain is controlled, infection treated, and INR stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my gynecologist and PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Get a chest X-ray in a few weeks. Call if fever, severe pain, or shortness of breath returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Nurse will go over your discharge instructions now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your transplant function is stable. Tacrolimus levels are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Keep taking your immunosuppressants as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—warfarin 2mg daily for two days, then INR check as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any other questions before discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think that’s everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in because your INR was low and you had a fall yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I fell off my horse—landed hard on my back. My head snapped down but I didn’t lose consciousness. They did a CT at the outside ER and said no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your INR was 1.7 when you got here. Because you have a mechanical mitral valve, we need your INR to stay above 3.0 for safety. That’s why we’re admitting you—to bridge with heparin until the warfarin catches up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve been on warfarin for years. Why did it drop this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not entirely sure yet. Sometimes changes in diet, fluid intake, or other meds can affect it. We’ll monitor closely and adjust your dose before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been eating less since the fall—my back and side really hurt. I’ve been taking tramadol and gabapentin like usual, but it’s not helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll reassess your pain and see what we can safely add. Given your kidney disease, some pain meds aren’t safe, but we’ll find a balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your INR is still low at 2.0. We’ve started IV heparin to protect your valve while we adjust the warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the heparin going to make me bleed? I’m on anticoagulants already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your blood work closely to avoid that. The heparin is temporary—just until your INR comes up safely with warfarin. We’ll check it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My back pain is still bothering me—can we try something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try a small dose of oral dilaudid, but we have to be very careful. With your kidney function, it can build up and affect your breathing or alertness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. I guess I’d rather be a little uncomfortable than risk something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a low dose of dilaudid earlier. The nurse mentioned you became very drowsy and your breathing slowed. We gave narcan to reverse it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember that… I just felt really out of it. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon in patients with kidney disease. The medication wasn’t clearing from your system, so it built up. We’ll avoid that med now and stick to safer options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad you caught it. Can we add something else for pain? Maybe more acetaminophen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can safely add acetaminophen. We’ll start 1000 mg every 8 hours. It’s safer for your kidneys and won’t affect your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had another episode of drowsiness last night after another dose. We gave narcan again. A CT of your head was done to rule out any bleeding—good news, it’s normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another one? I didn’t realize… So it’s definitely the medication, not a brain injury?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT shows no bleeding or injury. Your confusion and drowsiness are most likely from the dilaudid not clearing. We’ve stopped it completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. I was worried something was really wrong with my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were too, given your anticoagulation. But now we know it’s a medication effect. We’ll keep you on acetaminophen, tramadol, and gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is still impaired. You received dialysis yesterday, and we’ll continue your immunosuppressants and other ESRD meds as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My peritoneal catheter isn’t working well yet, is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not fully, no. It’s new, so it may take time. For now, we’re using your tunneled HD catheter for dialysis. We’ll follow up with your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 3.2—finally in the target range. We’re stopping the heparin and continuing warfarin at 5 mg daily for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good! So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We want to see one more INR to confirm it stays stable. And we need to make sure your pain is manageable at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m doing better with the new pain meds. Still sore, but I can move around with my walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest INR is 3.5—perfect. We’ll switch you to warfarin 2 mg daily to avoid it going too high, especially if your appetite stays low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower the dose if it’s finally in range?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your intake has been poor, and when you eat less, warfarin can become stronger. Lowering the dose helps prevent it from going too high once you’re home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ll be more careful with my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two clear head CTs, your mental status is normal, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I need help at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your recent fall and ongoing pain, we recommend a home health aide for a few days. We’ll help you apply for that service.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I don’t want to fall again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your labs are stable, you’re walking independently, and your INR is at 3.5. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take warfarin 2 mg every night. Check your INR tomorrow and call the coagulation clinic with the result. Continue your pain meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try the acetaminophen first. If it’s not enough, call your PCP. We’ll also suggest a pain management consult if it continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’ll follow up with my transplant team about the PD catheter too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your discharge instructions are ready, and the home health aide will contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better and safer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: warfarin 2 mg tonight, INR test tomorrow, and call the coagulation clinic. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And no more horseback riding for a while!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart plan. Let’s get you healed first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re doing well. Take it easy, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep an eye on the abrasion on your leg. Keep it clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been doing that. It’s not infected, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. Just keep it covered and monitor for redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll see you in follow-up if needed. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You're here today because you've been having trouble with fluid removal on peritoneal dialysis, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that's correct. I wasn’t getting enough volume off, and I was feeling bloated all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Because you're a rapid transporter, the peritoneal dialysis isn’t working as well for you. You’ve now switched to hemodialysis, which is going better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I feel more comfortable on hemodialysis. But I don’t need the old catheter anymore, so I’d like it removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve scheduled the removal for today. It’s a minor procedure, done under general anesthesia. Any questions before we go over the risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe with my heart condition and the mechanical valve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Because of your mechanical mitral valve, we need to manage your anticoagulation carefully. We’ll stop your warfarin and start a heparin drip after surgery to protect your valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then go back on warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Once we’re sure there’s no bleeding, we’ll restart warfarin and monitor your INR closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I’m ready to proceed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The PD catheter was successfully removed. The procedure went smoothly, and you tolerated anesthesia well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I feel groggy, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Normal after anesthesia. We’ve started the heparin drip as planned to protect your heart valve. Your warfarin is paused for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? I take tacrolimus and sirolimus for my transplants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are continuing as usual. We checked your levels this morning—tacrolimus was 3.8, which is within range. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my blood work? I know my counts are usually low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is 10.0, which is stable. White count was low at 2.2, but we’ve seen that before. We’re watching it, but no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. When can I start eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids today. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well overnight—stable vitals, no pain at the incision site. We’re going to restart your warfarin today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the heparin still running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the heparin will continue for now. We’ll overlap it with warfarin for a few days until your INR reaches the target.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should the INR be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For your mechanical valve, we aim for 2.5 to 3.5. We’ll check it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my dialysis? I’m used to my schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a session tomorrow—planned for 2 liters of fluid removal. Then you’ll go back to your regular outpatient unit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your INR is 2.1 this morning. It’s starting to rise. We’ll keep you on 6 mg warfarin daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that close enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s moving in the right direction. We expect it to reach 3.0 by tomorrow. Once it’s stable, we can talk about discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to go home. I feel fine—walking, eating, no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow, assuming your INR is in range and you complete dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a bowel movement this morning—finally. I used the suppository and extra Miralax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We were a bit concerned about constipation with the pain meds and reduced mobility. Good to see it’s resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I stop the heparin soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once your INR is above 2.0 for two days, we’ll stop the heparin. That should be tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is 3.0 this morning—perfect. You’ve completed your dialysis session with 2 liters removed. You’re medically ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual medications, including warfarin 6 mg daily. The coagulation clinic will follow your INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discontinue the drip now that your INR is therapeutic. No need for it anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What signs should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you develop a fever over 101, chills, or any redness, drainage, or bleeding at the incision site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially worsening pain. Also, keep checking your INR as instructed and follow up with the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll change the dressing daily, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Use clean technique and a new gauze each day. Let us know if it becomes wet or soiled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dialysis schedule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume your regular hemodialysis at your outpatient unit. They’ve been notified.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. We’ll arrange a chair car to take you home safely. Take care, and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge papers are ready. The instructions are all written down, including follow-up contacts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll review them when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to leave once transport arrives. We’ll miss you, but this is a good step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve recovered well from the procedure and are in stable condition. We’re confident you’ll do fine at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stay in touch with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having this sore on my left foot that won’t heal. It started after I hit my toe in the shower about a month ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And what happened after you hit it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It turned purple, and then my toenail fell off. It bleeds sometimes. I didn’t feel much pain because of my neuropathy, but my podiatrist said it looked bad and sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Given your history of diabetes and kidney disease, foot ulcers can be serious. We’ll need to check the blood flow to your leg and treat any infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Tomorrow, you’ll have a test called an angiogram to look at the blood vessels in your leg. After that, the vascular surgeon will decide if you need a procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m on dialysis too—will that affect anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll coordinate your dialysis. You’re scheduled for it the day after your angiogram. We’ll also monitor your kidney function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I have a mechanical valve and take warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know about that. We’ll start a heparin drip to keep your blood thin while we adjust your warfarin. Your INR will be checked daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you’re protected. For now, we’ll admit you, start IV antibiotics, and get some tests done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just got your chest X-ray back. It shows mild fluid in your lungs, but it’s stable. Your dialysis catheter and heart device are in good position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I sometimes feel short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your heart isn’t pumping as strongly as it should, so fluid can build up. We’ll manage that with your dialysis and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today is your angiogram. You’ll be taken shortly. Any questions before you go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be given sedation. You might feel some pressure, but not sharp pain. The team will use ultrasound to guide the catheter in your groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The angiogram is done. It went well. There’s a severe blockage in the artery of your left leg, which explains the poor healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the vascular surgeon recommends a left femoral endarterectomy. It’s scheduled for next week. You’ll be readmitted two days before to start heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing IV vancomycin. The urine culture showed contamination, so we’re focusing on the foot. Podiatry saw you and agreed to keep the offloading dressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to lose my toe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing everything to save it. Good blood flow after surgery and antibiotics should help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re due for dialysis today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My foot feels the same. The groin site is a little sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your labs show your INR is improving—now at 2.8. We’ll stop the heparin soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 3.1—perfect. We’ve stopped the heparin drip. You can stay on warfarin safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I eat regular food now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on a regular diet. We’ll keep monitoring your potassium and phosphorus due to your kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the foot X-ray back. No signs of bone infection, which is good. But there are changes from neuropathy and old fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no osteomyelitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not on the X-ray. If there’s still concern later, we might do an MRI, but for now, we’ll treat it as a soft tissue infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Afebrile, pain controlled, eating and walking. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What about the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get IV vancomycin on dialysis days until your follow-up. We’ve sent the prescription to your dialysis center.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot dressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the offloading pad on. Change the outer wrap if it gets dirty. See your podiatrist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. We’re comfortable discharging you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have fever, increased redness or drainage from the foot, or numbness or coldness in your leg. Also, watch the groin site for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the groin bleeds a lot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lie down, keep your leg straight, and press firmly for 10 minutes. If it doesn’t stop, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. We’ll review your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Continue all your usual meds except we’ve added IV vancomycin on dialysis days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And aspirin—discharge says 325 mg, but I was on 81 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good catch. For now, stay on 81 mg unless your surgeon says otherwise. I’ll correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can walk, shower, and do light activity. No heavy lifting for a week. And don’t drive while on pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll have help at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Follow up with Dr. Lee for your endarterectomy. We’ll admit you two days before to start heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll mark it on my calendar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—elevate your leg when sitting to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll use pillows like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done well. We’ll see you soon for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You can leave once transport arrives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember, call if you have any concerns before your surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will, I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis center has your vancomycin order. They’ll give it on your next session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I go Tuesday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s when the antibiotic is due.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you soon for your surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest and eat well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. See you next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the vascular surgery team. You've been admitted tonight because of the ulcers on your left foot and the blockage we saw in your leg artery last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember. The angiogram showed a bad blockage in my left leg, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It's a near-occlusive lesion in the left superficial femoral artery. We’re planning to fix that with a procedure called an endarterectomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a bypass? I thought I was getting a bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We initially planned a bypass using your own vein, but we need to check first if the vein is usable. That’s why we’re doing a vein mapping ultrasound tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. And what about my blood thinner? I’m on Coumadin for my mechanical valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re stopping your Coumadin for now and starting a heparin drip. That’s safer around surgery. We’ll restart Coumadin after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heparin will be adjusted based on my blood tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll monitor your PTT and adjust the drip to keep it in the right range. Once your INR is back up to 3.0–3.5, we’ll stop the heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll need dialysis too—usually on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve scheduled dialysis for tomorrow. The transplant nephrology team will be following you as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your vein mapping ultrasound was done this morning. The greater saphenous vein in your left leg is patent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we can use it for the bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll find out during surgery. Sometimes that vein was used in prior heart surgery and might not be available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a CABG years ago—could they have taken it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If it was harvested, we’ll have to use a different approach. But we have a backup plan—endarterectomy with patch angioplasty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as the blood flow gets fixed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little tired, but okay. No cramps this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep monitoring your labs, especially potassium and fluid status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your surgery for tomorrow morning. Any questions before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—what exactly is an endarterectomy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We open the artery and remove the plaque buildup. Then we sew in a patch to keep it open. It’s a direct way to fix the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll be in the ICU after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the VICU for one night, just to monitor your heart and circulation closely, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you're back from surgery. The procedure went well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did you use my vein for the bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We explored the greater saphenous vein, but it was tied off—likely used in your prior CABG. So instead, we did a femoral endarterectomy with patch angioplasty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that as good as a bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For your type of blockage, yes. It restores blood flow and should help your foot ulcers heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.8. We’re still running the heparin drip but getting close to stopping it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I be back on Coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already on it—4 mg daily. Once your INR hits 3.0–3.5 and stays there, we’ll stop the heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—am I back on all of them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, including tacrolimus, sirolimus, and aspirin. The transplant team reviewed everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The podiatry team cultured your foot ulcer today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was there an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture grew coagulase-negative staph. It’s a common skin bacterium, but we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need different antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You’re already on IV vancomycin on dialysis days, which covers it. We’ll continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your INR is now 3.9.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that too high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s slightly above our target of 3.0–3.5, but since we’re stopping the heparin today, it should stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. Can I start walking more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the physical therapist saw you today. You’re doing well. They recommend home physical therapy after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home nursing and physical therapy. You’ll need help with wound checks and mobility at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re healing well. The incision looks clean, no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry says it’s stable. Improved blood flow should help it heal over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a special diet too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2 grams sodium and 2 grams potassium. It’s important for your heart and kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that up at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have fever over 100.5, increased pain, redness spreading from the incision, or drainage that’s yellow or green.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can walk and go up and down stairs, but no heavy lifting—nothing over five pounds—for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, let water run over the incision, pat dry. No soaking in a tub yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. We’ve arranged home nursing, physical therapy, and your follow-up with Dr. Patel in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking Coumadin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 4 mg daily. Continue all your other meds too—especially the transplant and dialysis ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. The team is proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember: elevate your leg when sitting, eat small frequent meals, and keep up with your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And call if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your incision can stay uncovered unless there’s drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Just a dry dressing if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well and keep building your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping care for you during your stay. You’re here because of a foot ulcer and poor blood flow, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. The ulcer on my left foot has been getting worse, and it hurts a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve reviewed your history — you’ve had kidney and pancreas transplants, heart issues, and are on dialysis. We’ll need to be careful with treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I’m on a lot of meds. I also have a mechanical heart valve, so I’m always on blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re monitoring your INR closely. We did a vein mapping today to see if we can use a vein for bypass surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The small saphenous veins in both legs are open and could be used. But we’ll wait to decide after we treat your infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? I’ve had a cough and fever too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your chest X-ray shows some fluid buildup and early signs of pneumonia. That’s why we started antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know it was pneumonia. I’ve been coughing up yellow mucus and feeling chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits. We’re treating it as a healthcare-associated pneumonia. We started vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and flagyl.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were on 2 liters briefly, but your oxygen levels are better now. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show low white blood cells and high CRP, which means your body is fighting infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s expected with your immune status. We’re watching closely. Your kidney function is stable, and you’ll have dialysis today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my foot — will they do the surgery soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. With the fever and pneumonia, the vascular team wants to wait. We need you stable first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative so far. That’s good — no bacteria in the bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re helping, but your fever spiked to 102.6 last night. We’ve switched cipro to levaquin for better lung coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling achy all over. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common with systemic infection. We’ll keep managing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows worsening fluid in the lungs and a small left effusion. But no large pneumonia yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m still coughing. Is it getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cough is from irritation. We’ve added benzonatate to help. The good news is your oxygen levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to get a sputum sample, but it was too contaminated. We can’t tell if there’s a specific bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can’t you just guess from the X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating based on the most likely causes. The X-ray now shows left lower lobe consolidation — that’s pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics should clear it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re on vancomycin, levaquin, and flagyl — broad coverage. We’ll continue for 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your foot X-ray shows the ulcer but no bone damage. That’s good — no sign of osteomyelitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no bone infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that we can see. MRI could confirm, but clinically it doesn’t look like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still on hold due to pneumonia. Once you’re fever-free and stable, vascular will schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fevers are gone, and your cough is improving. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not quite. You still need IV antibiotics and wound care. Plus, your INR isn’t in range yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on heparin and warfarin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your INR was 2.5 this morning. We need it between 3.0 and 3.5 for your mechanical valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show improving kidney function and hemoglobin. Your CRP is coming down too — sign of less inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stable. Your transplanted pancreas is working well. We kept your tacrolimus dose higher and stopped sirolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why stop sirolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nephrology recommended it due to kidney concerns. Tacrolimus is safer for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is still 2.5. We’ll keep the heparin running until it reaches goal. You’ll go to rehab for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rehab? I thought I’d go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just for a short stay. They’ll check your INR daily and give IV antibiotics. It’s safer until your levels stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — your beta-D glucan test came back positive. It can suggest fungal infection, but it’s not specific.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I have a fungus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Infectious disease says your improvement on antibiotics points to bacterial pneumonia. We’ll follow up the test later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had enough to worry about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. Your pneumonia is resolving, and your foot ulcer is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue vancomycin IV during dialysis, plus oral flagyl and levaquin until the full 10-day course is done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the foot surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular will contact you to schedule revascularization after you recover. It’s key for healing the ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help with wound care, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll have home health nurses. Use the collagenase ointment daily and keep the dressing clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check it daily at rehab. Stay on heparin until INR is 3.0–3.5. Then they’ll stop the IV and adjust warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure they do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Keep up the good work, and follow up with all your specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest, and we’ll see you doing even better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — should I watch for any symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If you develop fever, increased cough, shortness of breath, or redness spreading around the ulcer, call your team right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And for chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it comes back or gets worse, especially with breathing, let us know. But it was likely from coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The discharge papers are ready, and transport will take you to rehab shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’m glad I’m on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take care, and we’ll follow up with your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I see you again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your primary and vascular teams will manage your follow-up, but I’ll send a full report. You’re in good hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s our job. Rest well, and keep up the progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — my nystatin. Is that for a yeast infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a precaution since you’re on antibiotics. Use it four times a day as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for clarifying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. That’s all for now. The nurse will help you get ready for transport.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. We're admitting you today for that non-healing ulcer on your left foot. Do you have any questions so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. Yes, I’ve been worried. Last time I was here, I got pneumonia and couldn’t have the procedure. Is it safe to do it now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great question. We reviewed your recent chest X-ray from earlier today. There’s clear improvement in the pneumonia. Your cough has mostly resolved, and you haven’t had fevers. So yes, we feel it’s safe to proceed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What exactly will you be doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do an angiogram to look at the blood flow in your left leg. Then, we plan to place a stent in the popliteal artery behind your knee to improve circulation to your foot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ulcer? Will that heal better after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Better blood flow helps wounds heal. We’ll keep up with daily dressing changes, and you’ll continue the collagenase ointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my transplant meds? I increased my tacrolimus to 2 mg twice a day after last discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve noted that. Transplant nephrology is involved, and we’ll check your tacrolimus levels every morning to keep it in the right range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also had some diarrhea off and on. Should I restart the loperamide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that. Since it’s not happening now, we won’t restart it yet. But if it returns, we can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my heart? I know I have the mechanical valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing your anticoagulation carefully. You’re on IV heparin now. Before the procedure, we’ll check your INR. If it’s too high, we may give fresh frozen plasma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. And after the stent, I’ll need both aspirin and coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. That helps keep the stent open. You’ll continue both long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when will the procedure happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. Today, we’ll do some final checks, including another set of labs and your dialysis session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had dialysis earlier today. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect timing. That helps us optimize your labs before surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot still feels very sensitive, even though I don’t have pain. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your history of diabetes and neuropathy, that’s common. We’ll keep protecting the area and checking pulses daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. The PTT is therapeutic at 70.7, so we’ll continue the heparin at 800 units per hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR? I know it was high last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was elevated, so we gave two units of fresh frozen plasma this morning. That should help bring it down before the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we’re back from the procedure. Everything went well. We placed a Zilver stent in your left popliteal artery and used a spider filter during the procedure to catch any debris.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Did the blood flow improve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the angiogram showed good flow after stenting. Your left foot has dopplerable pulses and is warm, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the groin site? Any issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We closed the access site with a Perclose device. No bleeding, and we’ll keep an eye on it for hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit tired. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. You’ll rest here for a few hours. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and restart your coumadin tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heparin will continue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart the IV heparin at 800 units per hour tonight and continue it until your INR is therapeutic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Your PTT is now 74.2, which is in the therapeutic range. We’ll discharge you today to extended care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: To rehab? Will they manage my heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll continue the IV heparin until your INR reaches the goal. You’ll keep taking aspirin and coumadin daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot? Should I keep it elevated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, elevate it above heart level when sitting. Avoid standing too long. And no heavy lifting for a week to protect the groin site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I call the office?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have new pain, coldness, or numbness in your leg, a fever over 101.5, or any bleeding from the groin. And keep up with your wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great. We’ll see you in follow-up in four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were brought in from another hospital with fever and a worsening infection in your left leg. Can you tell me how you're feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I'm in a lot of pain... it's burning and throbbing. I couldn't sleep last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I'm sorry you're hurting. We’ve given you some morphine for the pain. Your labs show a high white blood cell count and a very high CRP, which means there’s significant inflammation. We’re treating you for a serious skin infection called cellulitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that stent placed a few weeks ago. Is this related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. The stent improved blood flow, but poor circulation and diabetes make your foot vulnerable to infection. We’re also worried about possible bone infection, or osteomyelitis, especially since your toe looks necrotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Necrotic? You mean dead tissue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tip of your left toe has lost blood supply and the tissue is dying. That increases infection risk. We’ve started IV antibiotics—vancomycin and levofloxacin—to cover multiple bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate levofloxacin. It makes me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Infectious disease recommends it for now, but if it causes too much stomach upset, we can stop it. The vancomycin is the most important part.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… what about my blood thinner? I’m on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was dangerously high—10.1. That means your blood was way too thin. We gave you vitamin K to reverse it and prevent bleeding, especially since you had a bad headache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was so scared. I thought I was having a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your head, and there’s no bleeding or stroke. You’re safe. But we need to restart your anticoagulation carefully because of your mechanical mitral valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started a heparin drip to protect your heart valve while we get your INR back into the safe range—between 2.5 and 3.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney? I need dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve contacted dialysis. You’ll get treatment tomorrow. Your creatinine is stable, so your kidney function is as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been thinking… I’m so tired of all this. Sometimes I wonder if I should just stop dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big decision. We’ve asked psychiatry to speak with you to make sure you’re supported. They confirmed you have the capacity to make that choice, but we also started mirtazapine to help with depression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to die, but it’s so hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. We’re here to support you through this. Let’s focus on getting your infection under control first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures came back negative, which is good. But the outside hospital did grow Corynebacterium striatum. It’s often a contaminant, but we’re continuing antibiotics because you’re immunosuppressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bacteria that can sometimes cause real infection in people with transplants or weak immune systems. We’re not taking chances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my foot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an arterial study. Blood flow to your left foot is poor—especially in the posterior tibial artery, which is blocked. The stent is open, but disease is severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what can be done?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery recommends amputation of the affected toe. It could prevent the infection from spreading and avoid a bigger amputation later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Amputation? I’m not ready for that. Can I wait?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We respect that. You can go to rehab to recover and talk to your podiatrist. But know this: without surgery, the infection could worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—good sign the antibiotics are working. CRP is still high, but trending better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tacrolimus levels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They were high at first, so we lowered your dose from 2 mg to 1.5 mg twice a day. It’s now in the target range. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on tramadol and morphine. Can I go back to just tramadol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your pain is much better. We’ll stop the IV morphine and keep you on oral tramadol as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg is less red and no longer tender. The infection is improving. We’re continuing vancomycin through dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted warfarin at 2.5 mg daily. You’re still on the heparin drip to bridge until your INR is stable above 2.5 for 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home on the IV heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’ll go to extended care on the heparin drip temporarily. The anticoagulation clinic will help transition you fully to warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an angiogram yesterday. Blood flow to your foot is adequate for now, but the disease is severe. Vascular surgery still recommends amputation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I spoke with my podiatrist. I want more time to decide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll discharge you to rehab with a plan to continue antibiotics and follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm, the angiogram showed the stent is open and there’s enough flow to avoid emergency surgery for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your white count is almost normal, and the redness in your leg is gone. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue vancomycin through dialysis for five more weeks. Also levofloxacin, but stop it if it upsets your stomach. And warfarin with the heparin drip until your INR is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tacrolimus 1.5 mg twice daily, prednisone, and Bactrim for infection prevention. All your other home meds are continued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about the amputation decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a big decision. But know that delaying it could lead to worse outcomes. Please talk to your podiatrist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge to extended care. Your infection is much better, and your heart and kidney are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue IV vancomycin and oral levofloxacin. Take the levofloxacin after dialysis. Stop it if it causes nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the heparin drip continues until your INR is stable. The rehab team and anticoagulation clinic will manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my podiatrist next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
